claim: Serum amyloid A (SAA) is an evolutionally conserved protein family that has been conserved at least since the Cambrian period, from sea cucumber to human.
source: SAA is an enigmatic biomarker of inflammation that is better known as a protein precursor of systemic amyloid A (AA) amyloidosis, a life-threatening complication of chronic inflammation, than for its beneficial action (Westermark et al., 2015; Papa and Lachmann, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Uhlar et al., 1994 and Sun et al., 2016

claim: During acute-phase response, human SAA plasma levels increase swiftly more than 1,000-fold, reaching up to 3 mg/ml in 24–48 hr.
source: Remarkably, in acute inflammation, during infection, after injury or following surgery, plasma levels of SAA increase swiftly more than 1,000-fold, reaching up to 3 mg/ml in 24–48 hr, and then the levels drop (Sun et al., 2016; De Buck et al., 2016; Uhlar and Whitehead, 1999; Sack, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: SAA is produced mainly by the liver under the control of pro-inflammatory cytokines and is secreted into blood where it binds to high-density lipoprotein (HDL).
source: Inducible human SAA is produced mainly by the liver under the control of pro-inflammatory cytokines, is secreted into blood, and binds its major plasma carrier, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) (Benditt and Eriksen, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citation to Benditt and Eriksen, 1977

claim: SAA is also secreted locally at inflammation sites and is implicated in cytokine production and immune cell recruitment to these sites.
source: SAA is also secreted locally at inflammation sites and is implicated in cytokine production and immune cell recruitment to these sites (De Buck et al., 2016; Eklund et al., 2012; Ye and Sun, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: During the acute-phase response, human SAA isoforms 1, 2 and 3 are upregulated, while isoform 4 is constitutively expressed at much lower levels.
source: During the acute-phase response, which is a complex systemic response to severe inflammation, infection or injury (Gabay and Kushner, 1999), human SAA isoforms 1, 2 and 3 are upregulated (Uhlar and Whitehead, 1999), while isoform 4 is constitutively expressed at much lower levels (reviewed in Sun et al., 2016 and in De Buck et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published reviews and research articles

claim: Plasma levels of inducible SAA are elevated in infections such as tuberculosis, in autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Crohn's disease, and in certain cancers.
source: Plasma levels of inducible SAA are elevated in infections such as tuberculosis, in autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Crohn's disease, and in certain cancers (De Buck et al., 2016; Eklund et al., 2012; Ye and Sun, 2015; Sack, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Chronically elevated SAA is deleterious as a protein precursor of amyloidosis and as a causal risk factor for atherosclerosis.
source: Although chronically elevated SAA is deleterious as a protein precursor of amyloidosis and as a causal risk factor for atherosclerosis (Eklund et al., 2012; Getz et al., 2016; Thompson et al., 2018), the beneficial action of SAA is less clear.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: SAA can bind a range of apolar ligands, including cholesterol, retinol, phospholipids, lysophospholipids, and free fatty acids (FFA).
source: Free SAA can bind a range of other apolar ligands, including cholesterol (Liang et al., 1996), retinol (Derebe et al., 2014), phospholipids, lysophospholipids, and free fatty acids (FFA) (Takase et al., 2014; Jayaraman et al., 2015; Frame and Gursky, 2016; Tanaka et al., 2017; Jayaraman et al., 2017a; Frame et al., 2017; Jayaraman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: SAA binds various phospholipid vesicles and spontaneously solubilizes them to form HDL-sized particles de novo.
source: Our in vitro studies showed that SAA binds various phospholipid vesicles and spontaneously solubilizes them to form HDL-sized particles de novo (Frame et al., 2017; Jayaraman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' previous work

claim: The binding of diverse apolar ligands by SAA hinges upon a large concave apolar face of the SAA molecule formed by two amphipathic α-helices.
source: We proposed that this ability hinges upon the binding of diverse apolar ligands at a large concave apolar face of the SAA molecule (Frame and Gursky, 2016). This face, formed by two amphipathic α-helices, was observed in the atomic-resolution x-ray crystal structures of human SAA1.1 and murine SAA3 (Derebe et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to crystal structure studies and the authors' previous work

claim: Secretory PLA2 (sPLA2) group-IIa is an antimicrobial acute-phase reactant whose concentration in plasma and at inflammation sites can increase several hundred-fold simultaneously with that of SAA.
source: For example, sPLA2 group-IIa (sPLA2-IIa) is an antimicrobial acute-phase reactant whose concentration in plasma and at inflammation sites can increase several hundred-fold simultaneously with that of SAA (Pruzanski et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pruzanski et al., 1993

claim: sPLA2 is co-expressed with SAA and is induced by the same group of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Notably, sPLA2 is co-expressed with SAA and is induced by the same group of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Vadas et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vadas et al., 1993

claim: SAA stimulates smooth muscle cells to express sPLA2-IIa.
source: Moreover, SAA stimulates smooth muscle cells to express sPLA2-IIa (Sullivan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sullivan et al., 2010

claim: Clinical studies have reported a direct link between the plasma levels of SAA and the enhanced activity of sPLA2 during the early stages of inflammation.
source: Clinical studies have reported a direct link between the plasma levels of SAA and the enhanced activity of sPLA2 during the early stages of inflammation, whereas in vitro studies have shown that SAA enhances the remodeling of sPLA2-induced lipoproteins via an unknown mechanism (Pruzanski et al., 1995; Pruzanski et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pruzanski et al., 1995 and 1998

claim: sPLA2 hydrolyzes highly curved micelle-like surfaces in lipoproteins such as HDL (diameter 8–12 nm), but not intact planar bilayers.
source: Furthermore, sPLA2 hydrolyzes highly curved micelle-like surfaces in lipoproteins such as HDL (diameter 8–12 nm), but not intact planar bilayers (Høyrup et al., 2004; Halperin and Mouritsen, 2005), whereas SAA preferentially binds to such highly curved surfaces or forms them de novo by solubilizing lipid bilayers (Jayaraman et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: SAA solubilized POPC MLV (diameter circa 200 nm) to form smaller SAA-POPC complexes (~8 nm).
source: The results presented in Figure 1 show that SAA solubilized POPC MLV (diameter circa 200 nm) to form smaller SAA-POPC complexes (~8 nm).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: Increasing the SAA to POPC molar ratio from 1:100 to 1:10 increased the rate of solubilization and resulted in the generation of slightly smaller SAA-POPC particles.
source: Increasing the SAA to POPC molar ratio from 1:100 to 1:10 increased the rate of solubilization (Figure 1A) and resulted in the generation of slightly smaller SAA-POPC particles; for all ratios explored, the particle size was 7.5–8.5 nm (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: SAA-POPC particles were extensively hydrolyzed by sPLA2, whereas POPC MLV were not hydrolyzed by sPLA2.
source: In the absence of sPLA2, no significant hydrolysis of SAA-POPC particles was detected, but in the presence of sPLA2, extensive hydrolysis of the SAA-POPC particles was observed (Figure 1C). By contrast, MLV were not hydrolyzed by sPLA2: the levels of FFA were below the detection limit of our assay, and thin-layer chromatography showed only the presence of PC (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D

claim: SAA readily solubilizes model phospholipid bilayers such as POPC MLV and converts them into small HDL-size particles that provide excellent substrates for sPLA2.
source: Consequently, SAA readily solubilizes model phospholipid bilayers such as POPC MLV and converts them into small HDL-size particles that provide excellent substrates for sPLA2.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 1

claim: ApoA-I and apoA-II cannot spontaneously solubilize POPC MLV, unlike SAA.
source: This ability distinguishes SAA from other major HDL proteins, such as apoA-I and apoA-II, which cannot spontaneously solubilize POPC MLV (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: In SAA-POPC particles, approximately 70% of the total lipid was hydrolyzed by sPLA2-III and 60% by sPLA2-IIa.
source: In SAA-POPC particles, approximately 70% of the total lipid was hydrolyzed by sPLA2-III and 60% by sPLA2-IIa.
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental data in Figure 1C

claim: Human HDL containing various amounts of bound SAA (up to 27% of the total protein mass) showed a progressive increase in sPLA2 activity with an increasing amount of bound SAA.
source: Human HDL that contained various amounts of bound SAA (up to 27% of the total protein mass), termed SAA-HDL, were prepared by incubation of HDL with SAA using 1:1 or 4:1 protein weight ratio of exogenous SAA to endogenous apoA-I as described in the 'Materials and methods' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C). The lipoprotein fraction containing only HDL-bound proteins was isolated by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) from the total incubation mixture (marked SEC Fr and total in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and was hydrolyzed by sPLA2. A progressive increase in activity with an increasing amount of bound SAA was observed (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Free SAA augmented the lipolysis by sPLA2 of LDL.
source: To directly probe the role of free SAA, we incubated it with normal human LDL that does not bind SAA; the mixture (SAA +LDL, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) was hydrolyzed with sPLA2. Increased lipolysis was observed upon addition of free SAA to LDL (Figure 2C,D). Consequently, free SAA augmented the lipolysis by sPLA2 of various model and plasma lipoproteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: SAA enhances the hydrolysis by sPLA2-III or sPLA2-IIa of diverse substrates, including SAA-POPC complexes, plasma HDL, and plasma LDL.
source: In summary, the results in Figure 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D show that SAA enhances the hydrolysis by sPLA2-III or sPLA2-IIa of diverse substrates, including SAA-POPC complexes, plasma HDL, and plasma LDL.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from Figures 1 and 2

claim: SAA not only binds to phospholipid bilayers but also remodels them into smaller highly curved HDL-size particles (~8 nm) that are readily hydrolyzed by sPLA2.
source: This enhancement reflects the possibilities that: i) SAA not only binds to phospholipid bilayers but also remodels them into smaller highly curved HDL-size particles (~8 nm) that are readily hydrolyzed by sPLA2 (Figure 1D,E), and ii) SAA augments the action of sPLA2 in a manner that does not involve SAA binding to the substrate, as evident from the SAA-induced enhancement of LDL lipolysis (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from Figures 1 and 2

claim: All parent SAA-POPC particles of varying sizes (8 nm to 22 nm) were remodeled by sPLA2 into species that migrated at 7–7.5 nm.
source: SAA-POPC complexes that varied in size from about 8 nm to 22 nm were prepared by incubating SAA with POPC SUV at protein to lipid molar ratios ranging from 1:1 to 1:100. These incubation mixtures were hydrolyzed by sPLA2 for 3 hr at 37°C as described in 'Materials and methods'. Non-denaturing PAGE showed that all parent particles were remodeled by sPLA2 into species that migrated at 7–7.5 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Hydrolysis of native HDL by sPLA2 caused little change in the particle size distribution and no significant protein release.
source: Hydrolysis of native HDL by sPLA2 caused little change in the particle size distribution and no significant protein release (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Hydrolysis of SAA-HDL by sPLA2 led to lipoprotein remodeling into two major protein-containing species, of 10–12 nm and 7–7.5 nm in size.
source: By contrast, hydrolysis of SAA-HDL led to lipoprotein remodeling into two major protein-containing species, of 10–12 nm and 7–7.5 nm in size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: sPLA2 hydrolysis of SAA-POPC particles and SAA-HDL, but not of native HDL, leads to a release of protein-containing species that have a hydrodynamic size of 7–7.5 nm.
source: Together, the results in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 suggest that sPLA2 hydrolysis of SAA-POPC particles and SAA-HDL, but not of native HDL, leads to a release of protein-containing species that have a hydrodynamic size of 7–7.5 nm.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Regardless of the order of the events (binding to SAA and hydrolysis by sPLA2), SAA formed 7–7.5 nm complexes with the hydrolytic products of POPC.
source: Therefore, regardless of the order of the events (binding to SAA and hydrolysis by sPLA2), SAA formed 7–7.5 nm complexes with the hydrolytic products of POPC, suggesting that these complexes represented stable, kinetically accessible species.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Incubation of free SAA with sPLA2-treated HDL or LDL led to the formation of distinct 7–7.5 nm species.
source: Incubation of free SAA with sPLA2-treated HDL (Figure 3B) or LDL (Figure 3C) also led to the formation of distinct 7–7.5 nm species.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C

claim: The 7–7.5 nm species were released from parent lipoproteins only in the presence of both SAA and hydrolyzed phospholipids.
source: Such species were released from parent lipoproteins only in the presence of both SAA and hydrolyzed phospholipids, and were detected in model systems and in plasma lipoproteins (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C

claim: The ~7 nm species isolated from hydrolyzed SAA-HDL contain both SAA and apoA-I.
source: We used SDS PAGE and mass spectrometry to determine the protein composition of this isolated ~7 nm species. The results showed both SAA and apoA-I in the species released from the hydrolyzed SAA-HDL (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: Only SAA was detected in the ~7 nm species released from hydrolyzed LDL in the presence of SAA.
source: Only SAA was detected in the species released from hydrolyzed LDL in the presence of SAA (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D

claim: Both PC and lysoPC were observed in the ~7 nm species isolated from all hydrolyzed lipoproteins, including SAA-POPC, SAA-HDL, and SAA-containing LDL samples.
source: Lipid composition in this species was assessed by thin-layer chromatography and enzymatic assays. Both PC and lysoPC were observed in the ~7 nm species isolated from all hydrolyzed lipoproteins, including SAA-POPC, SAA-HDL, and SAA-containing LDL samples (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: FFA and phospholipid assays showed 30–45% FFA and 12–22% PC as a weight fraction of total lipids in the ~7 nm species.
source: FFA and phospholipid assays showed 30–45% FFA and 12–22% PC as a weight fraction of total lipids in these ~7 nm species.
evidence: Quantitative result from enzymatic assays

claim: SAA sequesters the FFA and lysoPC that are produced upon the lipolysis of diverse lipoproteins by sPLA2, and removes these hydrolytic products from the parent particle in the form of ~7 nm protein-lipid complexes.
source: We conclude that SAA sequesters the FFA and lysoPC that are produced upon the lipolysis of diverse lipoproteins by sPLA2, and removes these hydrolytic products from the parent particle in the form of ~7 nm protein-lipid complexes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 4

claim: The binding of SAA to POPC and other phospholipids induces α-helical folding in this intrinsically disordered protein at ambient temperatures, greatly increasing the thermal stability of SAA and protecting it from proteolysis.
source: Previous studies showed that the binding of SAA to POPC and other phospholipids induces α-helical folding in this intrinsically disordered protein at ambient temperatures, greatly increasing the thermal stability of SAA and protecting it from proteolysis (Takase et al., 2014; Jayaraman et al., 2015; Frame et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Far-UV CD spectra showed a major conformational change, from a largely unfolded secondary structure in free SAA to ~40% α-helix in complexes with lipids.
source: Far-UV CD spectra at 25°C showed a major conformational change, from a largely unfolded secondary structure in free SAA to ~40% α-helix in complexes with lipids.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The lipid-bound secondary structure was very similar in the parent SAA-POPC particles and in the ~7 nm products that are released upon lipolysis.
source: Notably, the lipid-bound secondary structure was very similar in the parent SAA-POPC particles and in the ~7 nm products that are released upon lipolysis (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The heating data for the precursor SAA-POPC particles and the ~7 nm product species partially overlapped and showed similar melting temperatures, Tm = 50 ± 2°C and 48 ± 2°C, respectively.
source: The heating data for the precursor particles and the ~7 nm product species partially overlapped and showed similar melting temperatures, Tm = 50 ± 2°C and 48 ± 2°C, respectively (Figure 5B), much higher than that of free SAA (Tm = 17 ± 2°C) (Jayaraman et al., 2015; Frame et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous work

claim: In the ~7 nm SAA complexes formed upon hydrolysis, the heating and cooling transitions were much closer than those in the precursor particles, and the hysteresis was nearly abolished.
source: Notably, in the ~7 nm SAA complexes formed upon hydrolysis, the heating and cooling transitions were much closer than those in the precursor particles, and the hysteresis was nearly abolished (Figure 5B, gray solid line).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Free SAA was largely fragmented within 5 min of incubation with trypsin at 22°C, whereas the ~7 nm complexes and their SAA-POPC precursor particles resisted proteolysis and underwent no major fragmentation even after 12 hr of incubation.
source: In contrast to free SAA, which was largely fragmented within 5 min of incubation with trypsin at 22°C (Figure 5C), the ~7 nm complexes and their SAA-POPC precursor particles resisted proteolysis, and they underwent no major fragmentation even after 12 hr of incubation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: SAA forms ~7 nm complexes with the hydrolytic products of sPLA2 that are distinct from free SAA and the SAA-POPC precursor particles.
source: Together, the results showed that SAA forms ~7 nm complexes with the hydrolytic products of sPLA2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5). Although these complexes migrate in the same size range as free SAA on the non-denaturing gel, their structure is distinct from that of either free SAA or the SAA-POPC precursor particles.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in multiple figures

claim: The ~7 nm complexes contain large amounts of FFA and lysoPC.
source: In contrast to precursors, these ~7 nm complexes: i) contain large amounts of FFA and lysoPC (Figure 4); ii) have smaller size (6.5–7.5 nm) and higher density (1.17–1.20 g/mL) indicative of a higher protein to lipid ratio; and iii) undergo a more thermodynamically reversible thermal unfolding (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: The ~7 nm complexes have smaller size (6.5–7.5 nm) and higher density (1.17–1.20 g/mL) indicative of a higher protein to lipid ratio compared to precursor particles.
source: In contrast to precursors, these ~7 nm complexes: i) contain large amounts of FFA and lysoPC (Figure 4); ii) have smaller size (6.5–7.5 nm) and higher density (1.17–1.20 g/mL) indicative of a higher protein to lipid ratio; and iii) undergo a more thermodynamically reversible thermal unfolding (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from density gradient centrifugation and non-denaturing PAGE

claim: The ~7 nm complexes undergo a more thermodynamically reversible thermal unfolding compared to precursor particles.
source: In contrast to precursors, these ~7 nm complexes: i) contain large amounts of FFA and lysoPC (Figure 4); ii) have smaller size (6.5–7.5 nm) and higher density (1.17–1.20 g/mL) indicative of a higher protein to lipid ratio; and iii) undergo a more thermodynamically reversible thermal unfolding (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The ~7 nm complexes released from hydrolyzed LDL in the presence of SAA contained SAA as their sole protein.
source: Instead, we focused on the ~7 nm complexes released from hydrolyzed LDL in the presence of SAA. Such complexes contained SAA as their sole protein (Figure 4C,D), facilitating a direct comparison with a model SAA-POPC system.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D

claim: Far-UV CD spectra of the ~7 nm complexes released from hydrolyzed LDL revealed a ~ 40% α-helical conformation, similar to that seen in the ~7 nm complexes released upon lipolysis of SAA-POPC.
source: Far-UV CD spectra of these complexes revealed a ~ 40% α-helical conformation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), similar to that seen in the ~7 nm complexes released upon lipolysis of SAA-POPC (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5A

claim: Thermal unfolding of the LDL-derived SAA-containing complexes was observed with Tm = 45 ± 2°C and was largely thermodynamically reversible.
source: Moreover, similar to these model complexes, thermal unfolding of the LDL-derived SAA-containing complexes was observed with Tm = 45 ± 2°C and was largely thermodynamically reversible (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The LDL-derived SAA-containing complexes resisted fragmentation upon incubation with trypsin at 22°C for up to 24 hr.
source: Finally, limited proteolysis ascertained the high conformational stability of SAA in these complexes, which resisted fragmentation upon incubation with trypsin at 22°C for up to 24 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: SAA sequesters the hydrolytic products of sPLA2 from model and plasma lipoproteins and forms stable ~7 nm complexes with these products.
source: We conclude that SAA sequesters the hydrolytic products of sPLA2 from model and plasma lipoproteins and forms stable ~7 nm complexes with these products.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figures 4 and 5

claim: SAA was previously shown to form spontaneously binary SAA-OA complexes that migrate at ~7.5 nm; the protein in these complexes was ~40% α-helical at 25°C and resisted tryptic digestion.
source: Upon incubation with OA, SAA was previously shown to form spontaneously binary SAA-OA complexes that migrate at ~7.5 nm; the protein in these complexes was ~40% α-helical at 25°C and resisted tryptic digestion (Jayaraman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jayaraman et al., 2018

claim: Non-denaturing PAGE showed SAA-lysoPC particles of ~8 nm in size, similar to those of SAA-POPC formed at 1:10 molar ratio of protein to lipid.
source: Non-denaturing PAGE showed SAA-lysoPC particles of ~8 nm in size, similar to those of SAA-POPC formed at 1:10 molar ratio of protein to lipid (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: Far-UV CD spectra showed substantial α-helical content in SAA-lysoPC particles, slightly lower than that in SAA-POPC particles (35% versus 40%).
source: Far-UV CD spectra showed substantial α-helical content in SAA-lysoPC particles, slightly lower than that in SAA-POPC particles (35% versus 40%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: Thermal unfolding of SAA-lysoPC particles was observed with Tm = 45°C, slightly lower than 50°C seen in SAA-POPC.
source: Thermal unfolding of SAA-lysoPC particles was observed with Tm = 45°C, slightly lower than 50°C seen in SAA-POPC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: SAA-lysoPC particles showed little hysteresis during thermal unfolding and refolding, unlike SAA-POPC particles.
source: Unlike SAA-POPC particles, SAA-lysoPC particles showed little hysteresis during thermal unfolding and refolding.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: SAA-lysoPC complexes resisted tryptic digestion, similar to other SAA-lipid complexes.
source: Moreover, similar to other SAA-lipid complexes, SAA-lysoPC complexes resisted tryptic digestion (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D

claim: SAA forms binary complexes with OA and with lysoPC where the protein is 35–40% α-helical and resists proteolysis at ambient temperatures.
source: Together, our results showed that SAA forms binary complexes with OA and with lysoPC. The protein in these complexes is 35–40% α-helical and resists proteolysis at ambient temperatures; the thermal unfolding is centered at Tm = 45–48°C and is largely thermodynamically reversible.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from Figure 5 and supplementary figures

claim: SAA can sequester POPC and its hydrolytic products, either separately or together, to form highly α-helical proteolysis-resistant complexes that are thermodynamically stable at ambient temperatures.
source: Clearly, SAA can sequester POPC and its hydrolytic products, either separately or together, to form highly α-helical proteolysis-resistant complexes that are thermodynamically stable at ambient temperatures.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 5 and supplementary figures

claim: The content of endogenous FFA in diabetic LDL was 20% higher than that in normolipidemic LDL.
source: LDL was isolated from the pooled plasma of subjects who were either normolipidemic or had diabetes mellitus, as previously described (Jayaraman et al., 2017b). The content of endogenous FFA in these diabetic LDL was 20% higher than that in normolipidemic LDL (Jayaraman et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jayaraman et al., 2017b

claim: SAA-containing ~7.5 nm complexes were released from diabetic as well as normolipidemic LDL upon incubation with SAA.
source: SAA was incubated with LDL using 1:1 weight ratio of SAA to apoB. Non-denaturing PAGE showed that the SAA-containing ~7.5 nm complexes were released from diabetic as well as normolipidemic LDL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), similar to those released from LDL upon hydrolysis by sPLA2 in the presence of SAA (Figure 3C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: SAA sequesters exogenous and endogenous FFA from lipoproteins to form similar-size complexes.
source: This result suggests that SAA sequesters exogenous and endogenous FAA from lipoproteins to form similar-size complexes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: In acute inflammation, plasma levels of albumin and its ability to sequester FFA and lysoPC decrease, while the levels of sPLA2 and SAA increase.
source: In acute inflammation, plasma levels of albumin and its ability to sequester FFA and lysoPC decrease, while the levels of sPLA2 and SAA increase (Gabay and Kushner, 1999; Pruzanski and Vadas, 1991; Fichtlscherer et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Both albumin and SAA removed a large portion of endogenous FFA from diabetic as well as normolipidemic LDL at pH 7.5, and albumin was slightly more efficient than SAA.
source: The results showed that both albumin and SAA removed a large portion of endogenous FFA from diabetic as well as normolipidemic LDL, and that albumin was slightly more efficient than SAA at pH 7.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: SAA can potentially contribute to FFA removal at plasma pH, albeit less efficiently than albumin.
source: This finding suggests that SAA can potentially contribute to FFA removal at plasma pH, albeit less efficiently than albumin.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: The SAA structure, stability and ability to remodel POPC MLV remain invariant at pH 7.5–5.5 but are altered at near-lysosomal pH.
source: Previously, we showed that the SAA structure, stability and ability to remodel POPC MLV remain invariant at pH 7.5–5.5 but are altered at near-lysosomal pH (Jayaraman et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jayaraman et al., 2017a

claim: Albumin was less efficient at removing FFA at acidic pH than at pH 7.5.
source: As expected, albumin was less efficient at removing FFA at acidic pH than at pH 7.5; this was evident from the higher residual content of FFA detected in LDL at pH 4.5–6.5 versus that at pH 7.5 (Figure 6, LDL + albumin).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: SAA's ability to remove FFA remained invariant at pH 4.5–7.5.
source: By contrast, SAA's ability to remove FFA remained invariant at pH 4.5–7.5 (Figure 6, LDL + SAA).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: At acidic pH, when the activity of albumin but not SAA was impaired, SAA removed more FFA than albumin per gram of protein.
source: Importantly, at acidic pH, when the activity of albumin but not SAA was impaired, SAA removed more FFA than albumin per gram of protein (Figure 6, LDL + SAA and LDL + albumin compared).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: SAA's role in FFA removal becomes particularly important at the acidic pH that are typical of inflammation sites.
source: This finding strongly supports the role of SAA in FFA removal in vivo and suggests that this role becomes particularly important at the acidic pH that are typical ofinflammation sites.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data in Figure 6

claim: Similar to mSAA1.1, hSAA1.1 spontaneously formed 8.5–9 nm particles upon incubation with POPC SUV at a 1:10 protein to lipid molar ratio.
source: Importantly, non-denaturing PAGE showed that, similar to mSAA1.1, hSAA1.1 spontaneously formed 8.5–9 nm particles upon incubation with POPC SUV at a 1:10 protein to lipid molar ratio (hSAA-POPC, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: Upon hydrolysis with sPLA2-IIa or sPLA2-III, hSAA1.1-POPC particles (8.5–9 nm) were remodeled into ~7.5 nm complexes.

claim: This in vitro study demonstrates that two ancient acute-phase plasma proteins, sPLA2 and SAA, act in synergy to break down and remove phospholipids.
source: This in vitro study demonstrates that two ancient acute-phase plasma proteins, sPLA2 and SAA, act in synergy to break down and remove phospholipids.

claim: SAA enhances the lipolysis by sPLA2 of diverse lipid assemblies, including model phospholipid vesicles as well as human HDL and LDL.

claim: SAA augments the sPLA2 reaction both by generating highly curved substrates for sPLA2 and by removing its reaction products, FFA and lysophospholipids.
source: We show that SAA augments the sPLA2 reaction both by generating highly curved substrates for sPLA2 (Figure 1) and by removing its reaction products, FFA and lysophospholipids (Figure 4).
evidence: Summary of experimental results from Figures 1 and 4

claim: Product removal determines the reaction rate of many lipases including sPLA2.

claim: Sequestration of membrane lipids and their degradation products by SAA and the safe removal of these bioactive products from the injured sites, which is a prerequisite for tissue healing, represents a vital role of this Cambrian protein.
source: Our results suggest that sequestration of membrane lipids and their degradation products by SAA and the safe removal of these bioactive products from the injured sites, which is a prerequisite for tissue healing, represents a vital role of this Cambrian protein.

evidence: Supported by citation to Pruzanski et al., 1996

claim: SAA is the only acute-phase protein that enhances the activity of sPLA2.
source: To our knowledge, SAA is the only acute-phase protein that enhances the activity of sPLA2.

claim: The in vivo synergy between SAA and sPLA2 is probably facilitated by the simultaneous secretion of these proteins systemically as well as locally at the inflammation sites.
source: The in vivo synergy between SAA and sPLA2 is probably facilitated by the simultaneous secretion of these proteins systemically as well as locally at the inflammation sites.

claim: Lipid sequestration by SAA is energy-independent.

source: Together, these findings suggest that during inflammation, when oxidative stress and lipolysis are increased, SAA augments the action of serum albumin by removing FFA, lysoPC, lipid peroxides and, potentially, other products of lipid degradation.

claim: The high stability of SAA complexes with lipids and their hydrolytic products contrasts with the marginal in vitro stability of lipid-free SAA oligomers at pH above pH 5.

claim: Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant whose plasma levels drop sharply in inflammation, with a concomitant steep increase in positive reactants, such as SAA and sPLA2.

claim: Cross-linking experiments with glutaraldehyde showed that intact SAA-POPC particles contained protein monomers, dimers and trimers, whereas hydrolyzed SAA-POPC showed a prominent hexamer band.
source: To assess the number of SAA molecules per particle, SAA-POPC particles were cross-linked with glutaraldehyde. SDS PAGE of intact SAA-POPC showed sharp bands corresponding to protein monomers, dimers and trimers, whereas hydrolyzed SAA-POPC showed a prominent hexamer band (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that each particle contained at least six protein molecules.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: Each hydrolyzed SAA-POPC particle contained at least six SAA molecules.
source: SDS PAGE of intact SAA-POPC showed sharp bands corresponding to protein monomers, dimers and trimers, whereas hydrolyzed SAA-POPC showed a prominent hexamer band (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that each particle contained at least six protein molecules.
